lines.1: He who possesses these six things, an army, a people, wealth, ministers, friends and a fortress, is a lion among kings
lines.2: Never to fail in these four things, fearlessness, liberality, wisdom, and energy, is the kingly character
lines.3: These three things, viz, vigilance, learning, and bravery, should never be wanting in the ruler of a country
lines.4: He is a king who, with manly modesty, swerves not from virtue, and refrains from vice
lines.5: He is a king who is able to acquire (wealth), to lay it up, to guard, and to distribute it
lines.6: The whole world will exalt the country of the king who is easy of access, and who is free from harsh language
lines.7: The world will praise and submit itself to the mind of the king who is able to give with affability, and to protect all who come to him
lines.8: That king, will be esteemed a God among men, who performs his own duties, and protects (his subjects).
lines.9: The whole world will dwell under the umbrella of the king, who can bear words that embitter the ear
lines.10: He is the light of kings who has there four things, beneficence, benevolence, rectitude, and care for his people
lines.11: Let a man learn thoroughly whatever he may learn, and let his conduct be worthy of his learning
lines.12: Letters and numbers are the two eyes of man
lines.13: The learned are said to have eyes, but the unlearned have (merely) two sores in their face
lines.14: It is the part of the learned to give joy to those whom they meet, and on leaving, to make them think (Oh! when shall we meet them again.)
lines.15: The unlearned are inferior to the learned, before whom they stand begging, as the destitute before the wealthy
lines.16: Water will flow from a well in the sand in proportion to the depth to which it is dug, and knowledge will flow from a man in proportion to his learning
lines.17: How is it that any one can remain without learning, even to his death, when (to the learned man) every country is his own (country), and every town his own (town) ?
lines.18: The learning, which a man has acquired in one birth, will yield him pleasure during seven births
lines.19: The learned will long (for more learning), when they see that while it gives pleasure to themselves, the world also derives pleasure from it
lines.20: Learning is the true imperishable riches; all other things are not riches
lines.21: To speak in an assembly (of the learned) without fullness of knowledge, is like playing at chess (on a board) without squares
lines.22: The desire of the unlearned to speak (in an assembly), is like a woman without breasts desiring (the enjoyment of ) woman-hood
lines.23: The unlearned also are very excellent men, if they know how to keep silence before the learned
lines.24: Although the natural knowledge of an unlearned man may be very good, the wise will not accept for true knowledge
lines.25: 51 The self-conceit of an unlearned man will fade away, as soon as he speaks in an assembly (of
lines.26: The unlearned are like worthless barren land: all that can be said of them is, that they exist
lines.27: The beauty and goodness of one who is destitute of knowledge by the study of great and exquisite works, is like (the beauty and goodness) of a painted earthen doll
lines.28: Wealth, gained by the unlearned, will give more sorrow than the poverty which may come upon the learned
lines.29: The unlearned, though born in a high caste, are not equal in dignity to the learned; though they may have been born in a low caste
lines.30: As beasts by the side of men, so are other men by the side of those who are learned in celebrated works
lines.31: Wealth (gained) by the ear is wealth of wealth; that wealth is the chief of all wealth
lines.32: When there is no food for the ear, give a little also to the stomach
lines.33: Those who in this world enjoy instruction which is the food of the ear, are equal to the Gods, who enjoy the food of the sacrifices
lines.34: Although a man be without learning, let him listen (to the teaching of the learned); that will be to him a staff in adversity
lines.35: The words of the good are like a staff in a slippery place
lines.36: Let a man listen, never so little, to good (instruction), even that will bring him great dignity
lines.37: Not even when they have imperfectly understood (a matter), will those men speak foolishly, who have profoundly studied and diligently listened (to instruction)
lines.38: The ear which has not been bored by instruction, although it hears, is deaf
lines.39: It is a rare thing to find modesty, a reverend mouth- with those who have not received choice instruction
lines.40: What does it matter whether those men live or die, who can judge of tastes by the mouth, and not by the ear ?
lines.41: Wisdom is a weapon to ward off destruction; it is an inner fortress which enemies cannot destroy
lines.42: Not to permit the mind to go where it lists, to keep it from evil, and to employ it in good, this is wisdom
lines.43: To discern the truth in every thing, by whomsoever spoken, is wisdom
lines.44: To speak so as that the meaning may easily enter the mind of the hearer, and to discern the subtlest thought which may lie hidden in the words of others, this is wisdom
lines.45: To secure the friendship of the great is true wisdom; it is (also) wisdom to keep (that friendship unchanged, and) not opening and closing (like the lotus flower)
lines.46: To live as the world lives, is wisdom
lines.47: The wise are those who know beforehand what will happen; those who do not know this are the unwise
lines.48: Not to fear what ought to be feared, is folly; it is the work of the wise to fear what should be feared
lines.49: No terrifying calamity will happen to the wise, who (foresee) and guard against coming evils
lines.50: Those who possess wisdom, possess every thing; those who have not wisdom, whatever they may possess, have nothing
lines.51: 54 Truly great is the excellence of those (kings) who are free from pride, anger, and lust
lines.52: Avarice, undignified pride, and low pleasures are faults in a king
lines.53: Those who fear guilt, if they commit a fault small as a millet seed, will consider it to be as large as a palmyra tree
lines.54: Guard against faults as a matter (of great consequence; for) faults are a deadly enemy
lines.55: The prosperity of him who does not timely guard against faults, will perish like straw before fire
lines.56: What fault will remain in the king who has put away his own evils, and looks after the evils of others
lines.57: The wealth of the avaricious man, who does not expend it for the purposes for which he ought to expend it will waste away and not continue
lines.58: Griping avarice is not to be reckoned as one among other faults; (it stands alone - greater than all)
lines.59: Let no (one) praise himself, at any time; let him not desire to do useless things
lines.60: If (a king) enjoys, privately the things which he desires, the designs of his enemies will be useless
lines.61: Let (a king) ponder well its value, and secure the friendship of men of virtue and of mature knowledge
lines.62: Let (a king) procure and kindly care for men who can overcome difficulties when they occur, and guard against them before they happen
lines.63: To cherish great men and make them his own, is the most difficult of all difficult things
lines.64: So to act as to make those men, his own, who are greater than himself is of all powers the highest
lines.65: As a king must use his ministers as eyes (in managing his kingdom), let him well examine their character and qualifications before he engages them
lines.66: There will be nothing left for enemies to do, against him who has the power of acting (so as to secure) the fellowship of worthy men
lines.67: Who are great enough to destroy him who has servants that have power to rebuke him ?
lines.68: The king, who is without the guard of men who can rebuke him, will perish, even though there be no one to destroy him

lines.70: It is tenfold more injurious to abandon the friendship of the good, than to incur the hatred of the many

lines.73: The power of knowing is from the mind; (but) his character is from that of his associates
lines.74: Wisdom appears to rest in the mind, but it really exists to a man in his companions
lines.75: Chaste company is the staff on which come, these two things, viz, purity of mind and purity of conduct
lines.76: To the pure-minded there will be a good posterity By those whose associates are pure, no deeds will be done that are not good
lines.77: Goodness of mind will give wealth, and good society will bring with it all praise, to men

lines.79: Future bliss is (the result) of goodness of mind; and even this acquires strength from the society of the good
lines.80: There is no greater help than the company of the good; there is no greater source of sorrow than the company of the wicked
lines.81: Let a man reflect on what will be lost, what will be acquired and (from these) what will be his ultimate gain, and (then, let him) act

lines.90: Let a man reflect, and do things which bring no reproach; the world will not approve, with him, of things which do not become of his position to adopt

lines.95: The axle tree of a bandy, loaded only with peacocks' feathers will break, if it be greatly overloaded
lines.96: There will be an end to the life of him who, having climbed out to the end of a branch, ventures to go further
lines.97: Let a man know the measure of his ability (to give), and let him give accordingly; such giving is the way to preserve his property
lines.98: Even though the income (of a king) be small, it will not cause his (ruin), if his outgoings be not larger than his income
lines.99: The prosperity of him who lives without knowing the measure (of his property), will perish, even while it seems to continue
lines.100: The measure of his wealth will quickly perish, whose liberality weighs not the measure of his property
lines.101: A crow will overcome an owl in the day time; so the king who would conquer his enemy must have (a suitable) time
lines.102: Acting at the right season, is a cord that will immoveably bind success (to a king)
lines.103: Is there anything difficult for him to do, who acts, with (the right) instruments at the right time ?
lines.104: Though (a man) should meditate (the conquest of) the world, he may accomplish it if he acts in the right time, and at the right place
lines.105: They who thoughtfully consider and wait for the (right) time (for action), may successfully meditate (the conquest of) the world
lines.106: The self-restraint of the energetic (while waiting for a suitable opportunity), is like the drawing back of a fighting-ram in order to butt
lines.107: The wise will not immediately and hastily shew out their anger; they will watch their time, and restrain it within
lines.108: If one meets his enemy, let him show him all respect, until the time for his destruction is come; when that is come, his head will be easily brought low
lines.109: If a rare opportunity occurs, while it lasts, let a man do that which is rarely to be accomplished (but for such an opportunity)
lines.110: At the time when one should use self-control, let him restrain himself like a heron; and, let him like it, strike, when there is a favourable opportunity
lines.111: Let not (a king) despise (an enemy), nor undertake any thing (against him), until he has obtained (a suitable) place for besieging him
lines.112: Even to those who are men of power and expedients, an attack in connection with a fortification will yield many advantages
lines.113: Even the powerless will become powerful and conquer, if they select a proper field (of action), and guard themselves, while they make war on their enemies
lines.114: If they who draw near (to fight) choose a suitable place to approach (their enemy), the latter, will have to relinquish the thought which they once entertained, of conquering them
lines.115: In deep water, a crocodile will conquer (all other animals); but if it leave the water, other animals will conquer it
lines.116: Wide chariots, with mighty wheels, will not run on the ocean; neither will ships that the traverse ocean, move on the earth
lines.117: You will need no other aid than fearlessness, if you thoroughly reflect (on what you are to do), and select (a suitable) place for your operations
lines.118: The power of one who has a large army will perish, if he goes into ground where only a small army can act
lines.119: It is a hazardous thing to attack men in their own country, although they may neither have power nor a good fortress
lines.120: A fox can kill a fearless, warrior-faced elephant, if it go into mud in which its legs sink down
lines.121: Let (a minister) be chosen, after he has been tried by means of these four things, viz,-his virtue, (love of) money, (love of) sexual pleasure, and tear of (losing) life
lines.122: (The king's) choice should (fall) on him, who is of good family, who is free from faults, and who has the modesty which fears the wounds (of sin)
lines.123: When even men, who have studied the most difficult works, and who are free from faults, are (carefully) examined, it is a rare thing to find them without ignorance
lines.124: Let (a king) consider (a man's) good qualities, as well as his faults, and then judge (of his character) by that which prevails
lines.125: A man's deeds are the touchstone of his greatness and littleness
lines.126: Let (a king) avoid choosing men who have no relations; such men have no attachment, and thereforehave no fear of crime
lines.127: Yields all his being up to folly's blind control
lines.128: Sorrow that will not leave even his posterity will come upon him chooses a stranger whose character he has not known
lines.129: Let (a king) choose no one without previous consideration; after he has made his choice, let him unhesitatingly select for each such duties as are appropriate
lines.130: To make choice of one who has not been examined, and to entertain doubts respecting one who has been chosen, will produce irremediable sorrow
lines.131: He should be employed (by a king), whose nature leads him to choose the good, after having weighed both the evil and the good in any undertaking
lines.132: Let him do (the king's) work who can enlarge the sources (of revenue), increase wealth and considerately prevent the accidents (which would destroy it)
lines.133: Let the choice (of a king) fall upon him who largely possesses these four things, love, knowledge, a clear mind and freedom from covetousness
lines.134: Even when (a king) has tried them in every possible way, there are many men who change, from the nature of the works (in which they may be employed)
lines.135: (A king's) work can only be accomplished by a man of wisdom and patient endurance; it is not of a nature to be given to one from mere personal attachment
lines.136: Let (a king) act, after having considered the agent (whom he is to employ), the deed (he desires to do), and the time which is suitable to it
lines.137: After having considered, "this man can accomplish this, by these means", let (the king) leave with him the discharge of that duty
lines.138: Having considered what work a man is fit for, let (the king) employ him in that work
lines.139: Prosperity will leave (the king) who doubts the friendship of the man who steadily labours in the discharge of his duties
lines.140: Let a king daily examine the conduct of his servants; if they do not act crookedly, the world will not act crookedly
lines.141: Even when (a man's) property is all gone, relatives will act towards him with their accustomed (kindness)
lines.142: If (a man's) relatives remain attached to him with unchanging love, it will be a source of everincreasing wealth
lines.143: 65 The wealth of one who does not mingle freely with his relatives, will be like the filling of water in a
lines.144: To live surrounded by relatives, is the advantage to be derived from the acquisition of wealth
lines.145: He will be surrounded by numerous relatives who manifests generosity and affability
lines.146: No one, in all the world, will have so many relatives (about him), as he who makes large gift, and does not give way to anger
lines.147: The crows do not conceal (their prey), but will call out for others (to share with them) while they eat it; wealth will be with those who show a similar disposition (towards their relatives)
lines.148: Many relatives will live near a king, when they observe that he does not look on all alike, but that he looks on each man according to his merit
lines.149: Those who have been friends and have afterwards forsaken him, will return and join themselves (to him), when the cause of disagreement is not to be found in him
lines.150: When one may have left him, and for some cause has returned to him, let the king fulfil the object (for which he has come back) and thoughtfully receive him again
lines.151: More evil than excessive anger, is forgetfulness which springs from the intoxication of great joy
lines.152: Forgetfulness will destroy fame, even as constant poverty destroys knowledge
lines.153: Thoughtlessness will never acquire fame; and this tenet is upheld by all treatises in the world
lines.154: Just as the coward has no defence (by whatever fortifications ha may be surrounded), so the thoughtless has no good (whatever advantages he may possess)
lines.155: The thoughtless man, who provides not against the calamities that may happen, will afterwards repent for his fault
lines.156: There is nothing comparable with the possession of unfailing thoughtfulness at all times; and towards all persons
lines.157: There is nothing too difficult to be accomplished, if a man set about it carefully, with unflinching endeavour
lines.158: Let (a man) observe and do these things which have been praised (by the wise); if he neglects and fails to perform them, for him there will be no (happiness) throughout the seven births
lines.159: Let (a king) think of those who have been ruined by neglect, when his mind is elated with joy
lines.160: It is easy for (one) to obtain whatever he may think of, if he can again think of it
lines.161: To examine into (the crimes which may be committed), to show no favour (to any one), to desire to act with impartiality towards all, and to inflict (such punishments) as may be wisely resolved on,
lines.162: When there is rain, the living creation thrives; and so when the king rules justly, his subjects thrive
lines.163: The sceptre of the king is the firm support of the Vedas of the Brahmin, and of all virtues therein described
lines.164: The world will constantly embrace the feet of the great king who rules over his subjects with love
lines.165: Rain and plentiful crops will ever dwell together in the country of the king who sways his sceptre with justice
lines.166: It is not the javelin that gives victory, but the king's sceptre, if it do no injustice
lines.167: The king defends the whole world; and justice, when administered without defect, defends the king
lines.168: The king who gives not facile audience (to those who approach him), and who does not examine and pass judgment (on their complaints), will perish in disgrace
lines.169: 68 In guarding his subjects (against injury from others), and in preserving them himself; to punish crime
lines.170: For a king to punish criminals with death, is like pulling up the weeds in the green corn
lines.171: The king who gives himself up to oppression and acts unjustly (towards his subjects) is more cruel than the man who leads the life of a murderer
lines.172: The request (for money) of him who holds the sceptre is like the word of a highway robber who stands with a weapon in hand and says "give up your wealth"
lines.173: The country of the king who does not daily examine into the wrongs done and distribute justice, will daily fall to ruin
lines.174: The king, who, without reflecting (on its evil consequences), perverts justice, will lose at once both his wealth and his subjects
lines.175: Will not the tears, shed by a people who cannot endure the oppression which they suffer (from their king), become a saw to waste away his wealth ?
lines.176: Righteous government gives permanence to (the fame of) kings; without that their fame will have no endurance
lines.177: As is the world without rain, so live a people whose king is without kindness
lines.178: Property gives more sorrow than poverty, to those who live under the sceptre of a king without justice
lines.179: If the king acts contrary to justice, rain will become unseasonable, and the heavens will withhold their showers
lines.180: If the guardian (of the country) neglects to guard it, the produce of the cows will fail, and the men of six duties viz, the Brahmins will forget the vedas
lines.181: He is a king who having equitably examined (any injustice which has been brought to his notice), suitably punishes it, so that it may not be again committed
lines.182: Let the king, who desires that his prosperity may long remain, commence his preliminary enquires with strictness, and then punish with mildness
lines.183: The cruel-sceptred king, who acts so as to put his subjects in fear, will certainly and quickly come to ruin
lines.184: The king who is spoken of as cruel will quickly perish; his life becoming shortened
lines.185: The great wealth of him who is difficult of access and possesses a sternness of countenance, is like that which has been obtained by a devil
lines.186: The abundant wealth of the king whose words are harsh and whose looks are void of kindness, will instantly perish instead of abiding long, with him
lines.187: Severe words and excessive punishments will be a file to waste away a king's power for destroying (his enemies)

lines.196: They resemble the trees of the earth, who although they have eyes, never look kindly (on others)

lines.499: A thorny tree should be felled while young, (for) when it is grown it will destroy the hand of the feller
lines.500: Those who do not destroy the pride of those who hate (them) will certainly not exist even to breathe
lines.501: Shade and water are not pleasant, (if) they cause disease; so are the qualities of (one's) relations not agreeable, (if) they cause pain
lines.502: Fear not foes (who say they would cut) like a sword; (but) fear the friendship of foes (who seemingly
lines.503: Fear internal enmity and guard yourself; (if not) it will destroy (you) in an evil hour, as surely as the tool which cuts the potter's clay
lines.504: The secret enmity of a person whose mind in unreformed will lead to many evils causing disaffection among (one's) relations
lines.505: If there appears internal hatred in a (king's) family; it will lead to many a fatal crime
lines.506: If hatred arises among (one's) own people, it will be hardly possible (for one) to escape death
lines.507: Never indeed will a family subject to internal hatred unite (really) though it may present an apparent union like that of a casket and its lid
lines.508: A family subject to internal hatred will wear out and lose its strength like iron that has been filed away
lines.509: Although internal hatred be as small as the fragment of the sesamum (seed), still does destruction dwell in it
lines.510: Living with those who do not agree (with one) is like dwelling with a cobra (in the same) hut
lines.511: Not to disregard the power of those who can carry out (their wishes) is more important than all the watchfulness of those who guard (themselves against evil)
lines.512: To behave without respect for the great (rulers) will make them do (us) irremediable evils
lines.513: If a person desires ruin, let him not listen to the righteous dictates of law, but commit crimes against those who are able to slay (other sovereigns)
lines.514: The weak doing evil to the strong is like beckoning Yama to come (and destroy them)
lines.515: Those who have incurred the wrath of a cruel and mighty potentate will not prosper wherever they may go
lines.516: Though burnt by a fire (from a forest), one may perhaps live; (but) never will he live who has shown disrespect to the great (devotees)
lines.517: If a king incurs the wrath of the righteous great, what will become of his government with its splendid auxiliaries and (all) its untold wealth ?
lines.518: If (the) hill-like (devotees) resolve on destruction, those who seemed to be everlasting will be destroyed root and branch from the earth
lines.519: Kings even fall from high estate and perish in the flame
lines.520: Though in possession of numerous auxiliaries, they will perish who are-exposed to the wrath of the noble whose penance is boundless
lines.521: Those who lust after their wives will not attain the excellence of virtue; and it is just this that is not desired by those who are bent on acquiring wealth
lines.522: The wealth of him who, regardless (of his manliness), devotes himself to his wife's feminine nature will cause great shame (to ali men) and to himself;
lines.523: The frailty that stoops to a wife will always make (her husband) feel ashamed among the good
lines.524: The undertaking of one, who fears his wife and is therefore destitute of (bliss), will never be applauded
lines.525: He that fears his wife will always be afraid of doing good deeds (even) to the good
lines.526: They that fear the bamboo-like shoulders of their wives will be destitute of manliness though they may flourish like the Gods
lines.527: Even shame faced womanhood is more to be esteemed than the shameless manhood that performs
lines.528: Those who yield to the wishes of their wives will neither relieve the wants of (their) friends nor perform virtuous deeds
lines.529: From those who obey the commands of their wives are to be expected neither deeds of virtue, nor those of wealth nor (even) those of pleasure
lines.530: The foolishness that results from devotion to a wife will never be found in those who possess a reflecting mind and a prosperity (flowing) therefrom
lines.531: The sweet words of elegant braceleted (prostitutes) who desire (a man) not from affection but from avarice, will cause sorrow
lines.532: One must ascertain the character of the ill-natured women who after ascertaining the wealth (of a man) speak (as if they were) good natured-ones, and avoid intercourse (with them)
lines.533: The false embraces of wealth-loving women are like (hired men) embracing a strange corpse in a dark room
lines.534: The wise who seek the wealth of grace will not desire the base favours of those who regard wealth (and not pleasure) as (their) riches
lines.535: Those whose knowledge is made excellent by their (natural) sense will not covet the trffling delights
lines.536: Those who would spread (the fame of) their own goodness will not desire the shoulders of those,who rejoice in their accomplishments and bestow their despicable favours (on all who pay)
lines.537: Those who are destitute of a perfectly (reformed) mind will covet the shoulders of those who embrace (them) while their hearts covet other things
lines.538: The wise say that to such as are destitute of discerning sense the embraces of faithless women are (as ruinous as those of) the celestail female
lines.539: The delicate shoulders of prostitutes with excellent jewels are a hell into which are plunged the ignorant base
lines.540: Treacherous women, liquor, and gambling are the associates of such as have forsaken by Fortune
lines.541: Those who always thirst after drink will neither inspire fear (in others) nor retain the light (of their fame)
lines.542: Let no liquor be drunk; if it is desired, let it be drunk by those who care not for esteem of the great
lines.543: Intoxication is painful even in the presence of (one's) mother; what will it not then be in that of the wise ?
lines.544: The fair maid of modesty will turn her back on those who are guilty of the great and abominable crime of drunkenness
lines.545: To give money and purchase unconsciousness is the result of one's ignorance of (one's own actions)
lines.546: They that sleep resemble the deed; (likewise) they that drink are no other than poison-eaters
lines.547: Those who always intoxicate themselves by a private (indulgence in) drink; will have their secrets detected and laughed at by their fellow-townsmen
lines.548: Let (the drunkard) give up saying "I have never drunk"; (for) the moment (he drinks) he will simply betray his former attempt to conceal
lines.549: Reasoning with a drunkard is like going under water with a torch in search of a drowned man
lines.550: When (a drunkard) who is sober sees one who is not, it looks as if he remembered not the evil effects of his (own) drink
lines.551: Though able to win, let not one desire gambling; (for) even what is won is like a fish swallowing the iron in fish-hook
lines.552: That they may good obtain, and see a prosperous day? Is there indeed a means of livelihood that can bestow happiness on gamblers who gain one and lose a hundred?
lines.553: If the king is incessantly addicted to the rolling dice in the hope of gain, his wealth and the resources thereof will take their departure and fall into other's hands
lines.554: There is nothing else that brings (us) poverty like gambling which causes many a misery and destroys (one's) reputation
lines.555: Penniless are those who by reason of their attachment would never forsake gambling, the gamblingplace and the handling (of dice)
lines.556: Those who are swallowed by the goddess called "gambling" will never have their hunger satisfied, but suffer the pangs of hell in the next world
lines.557: To waste time at the place of gambling will destroy inherited wealth and goodness of character
lines.558: Gambling destroys property, teaches falsehood, puts an end to benevolence, and brings in misery (here and hereafter)
lines.559: The habit of gambling prevents the attainment of these five: clothing, wealth, food, fame and learning
lines.560: As the gambler loves (his vice) the more he loses by it, so does the soul love (the body) the more it suffers through it
lines.561: If (food and work are either) excessive or deficient, the three things enumerated by (medical) writers, flatulence, biliousness, and phlegm, will cause (one) disease
lines.562: No medicine is necessary for him who eats after assuring (himself) that what he has (already) eaten has been digested
lines.563: If (one's food has been) digested let one eat with moderation; (for) that is the way to prolong the life of an embodied soul
lines.564: (First) assure yourself that your food has been digested and never fail to eat, when very hungry, whatever is not disagreeable (to you)
lines.565: There will be no disaster to one's life if one eats with moderation, food that is not disagreeable
lines.566: As pleasure dwells with him who eats moderately, so disease (dwells) with the glutton who eats voraciously
lines.567: He will be afflicted with numberless diseases, who eats immoderately, ignorant (of the rules of health)
lines.568: Let the physician enquire into the (nature of the) disease, its cause and its method of cure and treat it faithfully according to (medical rule)
lines.569: The learned (physician) should ascertain the condition of his patient; the nature of his disease, and the season (of the year) and (then) proceed (with his treatment)
lines.570: Medical science consists of four parts, viz, patient, physician, medicine and compounder; and each of these (again) contains four sub-divisions
lines.571: Consistency (of thought, word and deed) and fear (of sin) are conjointly natural only to the high-born
lines.572: The high-born will never deviate from these three; good manners, truthfulness and modesty
lines.573: A cheerful countenance, liberality, pleasant words, and an unreviling disposition, these four are said to be the proper qualities of the truly high-born
lines.574: Though blessed with immense wealth, the noble will never do anything unbecoming
lines.575: Though their means fall off, those born in ancient families, will not lose their character (for liberality)
lines.576: Those who seek to preserve the irreproachable honour of their families will not viciously do what is detrimental thereto
lines.577: As spots on her bright orb that walks sublime the evening sky
lines.578: If one of a good family betrays want of affection, his descent from it will be called in question
lines.579: As the sprout indicates the nature of the soil, (so) the speech of the noble indicates (that of one's birth)
lines.580: He who desires a good name must desire modesty; and he who desires (the continuance of) a family greatness must be submissive to all
lines.581: Actions that would degrade (one's) family should not be done; though they may be so important that not doing them would end in death
lines.582: Those who desire (to maintain their) honour, will surely do nothing dishonourable, even for the sake of fame
lines.583: In great prosperity humility is becoming; dignity, in great adversity
lines.584: They who have fallen from their (high) position are like the hair which has fallen from the head
lines.585: Even those who are exalted like a hill will be thought low, if they commit deeds that are debasing
lines.586: Why follow men who scorn, and at their bidding wait?
lines.587: It is better for a man to be said of him that he died in his usual state than that he eked out his life by following those who disgraced him
lines.588: For the high-born to keep their body in life when their honour is gone will certainly not prove a remedy against death
lines.589: Those who give up (their) life when (their) honour is at stake are like the yark which kills itself at the loss of (even one of) its hairs
lines.590: The world will (always) praise and adore the fame of the honourable who would rather die than suffer indignity
lines.591: One's light is the abundance of one's courage; one's darkness is the desire to live destitute of such (a state of mind.)
lines.592: All human beings agree as regards their birth but differ as regards their characteristics, because of the different qualities of their actions
lines.593: Though (raised) above, the base cannot become great; though (brought) low, the great cannot become base
lines.594: Exists while to itself is true
lines.595: (Though reduced) the great will be able to perform, in the proper way, deeds difficult (for others to do)
lines.596: It is never in the nature of the base to seek the society of the great and partake of their nature
lines.597: Even nobility of birth, wealth and learning, if in (the possession of) the base, will (only) produce everincreasing pride
lines.598: The great will always humble himself; but the mean will exalt himself in self-admiration
lines.599: Freedom from conceit is (the nature of true) greatness; (while) obstinacy therein is (that of) meanness
lines.600: The great hide the faults of others; the base only divulge them
lines.601: It is said that those who are conscious of their duty and behave with a perfect goodness will regard as natural all that is good
lines.602: The only delight of the perfect is that of their goodness; all other (sensual) delights are not to be included among any (true) delights
lines.603: Affection, fear (of sin), benevolence, favour and truthfulness; these are the five pillars on which perfect goodness rests
lines.604: Penance consists in the goodness that kills not , and perfection in the goodness that tells not others' faults
lines.605: Stooping (to inferiors) is the strength of those who can accomplish (an undertaking); and that is the weapon with which the great avert their foes
lines.606: The touch-stone of perfection is to receive a defeat even at the hands of one's inferiors
lines.607: Of what avail is perfect goodness if it cannot do pleasing things even to those who have pained (it) ?
lines.608: Poverty is no disgrace to one who abounds in good qualities
lines.609: Those who are said to be the shore of the sea of perfection will never change, though ages may change
lines.610: If there is a defect in the character of the perfect, (even) the great world cannot bear (its) burden
lines.611: If one is easy of access to all, it will be easy for one to obtain the virtue called goodness
lines.612: Affectionateness and birth in a good family, these two constitute what is called a proper behaviour to all
lines.613: Resemblance of bodies is no resemblance of souls; true resemblance is the resemblance of qualities that attract
lines.614: The world applauds the character of those whose usefulness results from their equity and charity
lines.615: Reproach is painful to one even in sport; those (therefore) who know the nature of others exhibit (pleasing) qualities even when they are hated
lines.616: The (way of the) world subsists by contact with the good; if not, it would bury itself in the earth and perish
lines.617: He who is destitute of (true) human qualities (only) resembles a tree, though he may possess the sharpness of a file
lines.618: It is wrong (for the wise) not to exhibit (good) qualities even towards those who bearing no friendship (for them) do only what is hateful
lines.619: To those who cannot rejoice, the wide world is buried darkness even in (broad) day light
lines.620: The great wealth obtained by one who has no goodness will perish like pure milk spoilt by the
lines.621: He who does not enjoy the immense riches he has heaped up in his house, is (to be reckoned as) dead, (for) there is nothing achieved (by him)
lines.622: He who knows that wealth yields every pleasure and yet is so blind as to lead miserly life will be born a demon
lines.623: A burden to the earth are men bent on the acquisition of riches and not (true) fame
lines.624: What will the miser who is not liked (by any one) regard as his own (in the world to come) ?
lines.625: Those who neither give (to others) nor enjoy (their property) are (truly) destitute, though possessing immense riches
lines.626: He who enjoys not (his riches) nor relieves the wants of the worthy is a disease to his wealth
lines.627: The wealth of him who never bestows anything on the destitute is like a woman of beauty growing old without a husband
lines.628: The wealth of him who is disliked (by all) is like the fruit-bearing of the etty tree in the midst of a town
lines.629: To heap up glittering wealth, their hoards shall others take
lines.630: The short-lived poverty of those who are noble and rich is like the clouds becoming poor (for a while)
lines.631: True modesty is the fear of (evil) deeds; all other modesty is (simply) the bashfulness of virtuous maids
lines.632: Food, clothing and the like are common to all men but modesty is peculiar to the good
lines.633: As the body is the abode of the spirit, so the excellence of modesty is the abode of perfection
lines.634: Is not the modesty ornament of the noble ? Without it, their haughtiness would be a pain (to others)
lines.635: The world regards as the abode of modesty him who fear his own and other's guilt
lines.636: The great make modesty their barrier (of defence) and not the wide world
lines.637: The modest would rather lose their life for the sake of modesty than lose modesty for the sake of life
lines.638: Virtue is likely to forsake him who shamelessly does what others are ashamed of
lines.639: Want of manners injures one's family; but want of modesty injures one's character
lines.640: The actions of those who are without modesty at heart are like those of puppet moved by a string
lines.641: There is no higher greatness than that of one saying I will not cease in my effort (to raise my family)
lines.642: One's family is raised by untiring perseverance in both effort and wise contrivances
lines.643: The Deity will clothe itself and appear before him who resolves on raising his family
lines.644: Those who are prompt in their efforts (to better their family) need no deliberation, such efforts will of themselves succeed
lines.645: People will eagerly seek the friendship of the prosperous soul who has raised his family without foul means
lines.646: A man's true manliness consists in making himself the head and benefactor of his family
lines.647: Amid his kindred so the burthen rests upon the strong
lines.648: As a family suffers by (one's) indolence and false dignity there is to be so season (good or bad) to those who strive to raise their family
lines.649: Is it only to suffering that his body is exposed who undertakes to preserve his family from evil ?
lines.650: If there are none to prop up and maintain a family (in distress), it will fall at the stroke of the axe of misfortune
lines.651: Agriculture, though laborious, is the most excellent (form of labour); for people, though they go about (in search of various employments), have at last to resort to the farmer
lines.652: Agriculturists are (as it were) the linch-pin of the world for they support all other workers who cannot till the soil
lines.653: They alone live who live by agriculture; all others lead a cringing, dependent life
lines.654: Patriotic farmers desire to bring all other states under the control of their own king
lines.655: Those whose nature is to live by manual labour will never beg but give something to those who beg
lines.656: If the farmer's hands are slackened, even the ascetic state will fail
lines.657: If the land is dried so as to reduce one ounce of earth to a quarter, it will grow plentifully even without a handful of manure
lines.658: Manuring is better than ploughing; after weeding, watching is better than watering (it)
lines.659: If the owner does not (personally) attend to his cultivation, his land will behave like an angry wife and yield him no pleasure
lines.660: The maiden, Earth, will laugh at the sight of those who plead poverty and lead an idle life
lines.661: There is nothing that afflicts (one) like poverty
lines.662: When cruel poverty comes on, it deprives one of both the present and future (bliss)
lines.663: Hankering poverty destroys at once the greatness of (one's) ancient descent and (the dignity of one's) speech
lines.664: Even in those of high birth, poverty will produce the fault of uttering mean words
lines.665: The misery of poverty brings in its train many (more) miseries
lines.666: The words of the poor are profitless, though they may be sound in thought and clear in expression
lines.667: He that is reduced to absolute poverty will be regarded as a stranger even by his own mother
lines.668: Is the poverty that almost killed me yesterday, to meet me today too ?
lines.669: One may sleep in the midst of fire; but by no means in the midst of poverty
lines.670: The destitute poor, who do not renounce their bodies, only consume their neighbour's salt and water
lines.671: If you meet with those that may be begged of, you may beg; (but) if they withhold (their gift) it is their blame and not yours
lines.672: Even begging may be pleasant, if what is begged for is obtained without grief (to him that begs)
lines.673: There is even a beauty in standing before and begging of those who are liberal in their gifts and understand their duty (to beggars)
lines.674: To beg of such as never think of withholding (their charity) even in their dreams, is in fact the same as giving (it oneself);
lines.675: As there are in the world those that give without refusing, there are (also) those that prefer to beg by simply standing before them
lines.676: All the evil of begging will be removed at the sight of those who are far from the evil of refusing
lines.677: Beggars rejoice exceedingly when they behold those who bestow (their alms) with kindness and courtesy
lines.678: If there were no beggars, (the actions done in) the cool wide world would only resemble the movement of a puppet
lines.679: What (praise) would there be to givers (of alms) if there were no beggars to ask for and reveive (them)
lines.680: He who begs ought not to be angry (at a refusal); for even the misery of (his own) poverty should be a sufficient reason (for so doing)
lines.681: Not to beg (at all) even from those excellent persons who cheerfully give without refusing, will do immense good
lines.682: If the Creator of the world has decreed even begging as a means of livelihood, may he too go abegging and perish
lines.683: There is no greater folly than the boldness with which one seeks to remedy the evils of poverty by begging (rather than by working)
lines.684: Even the whole world cannot sufficiently praise the dignity that would not beg even in the midst of destitution
lines.685: Even thin gruel is ambrosia to him who has obtained it by labour
lines.686: There is nothing more disgraceful to one's tongue than to use it in begging water even for a cow
lines.687: I beseech all beggars and say, "If you need to beg, never beg of those who give unwillingly."
lines.688: The unsafe raft of begging will split when it strikes on the rock of refusal
lines.689: To think of (the evil of) begging is enough to melt one's heart; but to think of refusal is enough to break it
lines.690: Saying "No" to a beggar takes away his life. (but as that very word will kill the refuser) where then would the latter's life hide itself ?
lines.691: The base resemble men perfectly (as regards form); and we have not seen such (exact) resemblance (among any other species)
lines.692: The low enjoy more felicity than those who know what is good; for the former are not troubled with anxiety (as to the good)
lines.693: The base resemble the Gods; for the base act as they like
lines.694: The base feels proud when he sees persons whose acts meaner than his own
lines.695: (The principle of) behaviour in the mean is chiefly fear; if not, hope of gain, to some extent
lines.696: The base are like a drum that is beaten, for they unburden to others the secrets they have heard
lines.697: The mean will not (even) shake off (what sticks to) their hands (soon after a meal) to any but those who would break their jaws with their clenched fists
lines.698: The great bestow (their alms) as soon as they are informed; (but) the mean, like the sugar-cane, only when they are tortured to death
lines.699: The base will bring an evil (accusation) against others, as soon as he sees them (enjoying) good food
lines.700: The base will hasten to sell themselves as soon as a calamity has befallen them. For what else are they fitted ?
